item.title: Should You Invest in Anthropic? Here’s What to Consider.
item.description:
Buying into Anthropic doesn’t feel like your typical single-stock bet.

Unlike many initial public offering disclosure forms, this one won’t put you to sleep — but it may drive you to reach for a Xanax.

The artificial intelligence company, which on Thursday was the first A.I. lab to go public, explains the singular wager its investors are making in its prospectus, the regulatory filing that describes a new company’s business strategy, prospects and risks.

It lays out its great promise (curing diseases like cancer, developing drugs and other revolutionary innovations) and its most perilous downsides, among them “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."

The notion of existential risk hasn’t prevented investors from piling into the shares of the company, valued at $1.5 trillion, which released roughly 6 percent of its shares overall to the public. Demand was far higher: The stock was priced at $83 a share, above its original target of $70 to $78, and opened trading at $111.50, a 34 percent jump.

Placing a significant portion of your wealth on a single stock is never a good idea, but there’s always the temptation to buy something when a shiny new offering comes along. Research still shows that keeping a diversified mix of stocks and bonds over the long-term is the best bet you can make.

But if you’re considering Anthropic, here are several questions to ask yourself first.

If you hold U.S. stock index funds, you’re probably already investing in A.I. — and you’re arguably even overexposed. About 35 percent of the holdings that the Morningstar Total Stock Index tracks, for example, are directly related to some type of A.I. play, according to Rodney Comegys, chief investment officer of Vanguard Capital Management and head of global equity.

That includes so-called hyperscalers, or companies like Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta that operate vast computing and data infrastructure; chip suppliers like Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices; among other categories.

Another proxy is to look at how much money your funds have allocated to the so-called Magnificent Seven, or the seven largest tech holdings, some of which have invested in Anthropic or are otherwise interconnected to the industry. This group accounts for more than a quarter of U.S. stock index funds that track the entire market, and more than a third of the S&P 500. This collection also drove 46 percent of the S&P 500’s overall return in 2025, according to J.P. Morgan Asset Management, and 55 percent in 2024, underscoring just how much they’re buoying overall performance.

Many U.S. stock index fund investors will also automatically own Anthropic stock before too long, as soon as the next week, though the initial amount will be small. Index funds try to reflect the entire stock market — so many of them will incorporate Anthropic based on the amount of shares that are publicly available.

Anthropic’s stock will initially account for an estimated 0.05 percent to 0.15 percent of the Vanguard Total Stock Market, for example, though that is likely to grow over time.

Other index funds don’t move as quickly. Funds that track the S&P 500 Index, for example, generally follow a different set of rules, which has a 12-month waiting period but also requires companies to meet profitability hurdles.

There may also be other companies that are helped (or hurt) by A.I., just as different businesses were revolutionized by the internet.

“If you look 20 years later, the companies that benefit the most from the internet worlds are something like a Home Depot or a Walmart,” Mr. Comegys added, which helped improve supply chains and sales.

Financial journalists are prohibited from investing in companies we write about. The last time I can remember buying an individual stock — Krispy Kreme! — was not long after the first tech boom. That purchase felt like an old-fashioned, Warren Buffett brand of capitalism — a company you could generally understand, and the big risk was that the chain would grow too fast.

How much can any average person truly understand about a company as complex as Anthropic, along with its founders? When you make a single bet, you’re also betting on the company’s leaders. After Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say is an asset for Chinese intelligence became public this month, its stock plummeted. Since its peak in October, the company has given up a third, or $2 trillion, of its market value.

There’s a lot we won’t know, even if our policymakers demand more transparency and regulation.

In September, an Anthropic researcher who previously worked at OpenAI said he resigned from Anthropic because he felt “neither company is acting responsibly.”

One of Anthropic’s billionaire founders recently tried to convince religious scholars that Claude could become conscious.

It’s a lot to process.

Stocks that make splashy debuts can be disappointing performers, at least for a while. Investors are essentially paying $42 for each dollar of Anthropic’s revenue. Similar companies that cost more than $40 for each dollar of revenue have underperformed the broader market in the three years after their I.P.O., even for investors who bought at the offer price, according to an analysis by Jay Ritter, an I.P.O. expert at the University of Florida. (New technology offerings overall, however, tended to outperform non-tech I.P.O.s during that same time period.)

“With Anthropic, and for that matter, SpaceX,” he said, “the valuations are reflecting very optimistic assumptions.” He added, “This time could be different, because these are companies, Anthropic in particular, with game-changing technology that’s not easy to duplicate.”

Several brokerage firms — Charles Schwab, E*Trade, Fidelity, Robinhood, SoFi and others — had access to a portion of the initial shares, and were offering customers the chance to acquire them at the I.P.O. price. But there were no guarantees that all customers who expressed interest would receive them.

Each firm had different rules on how they would be allocated. At Fidelity and Schwab, for example, customers needed to have at least $25,000 and $50,000 in assets, respectively, to participate.

Many financial planners have said it’s perfectly fine to take a small portion of your overall stock portfolio, say 5 percent, for play money and placing bets — as long as the rest of your savings remains diversified and thoughtfully positioned to meet specific longer-term goals, whether for retirement or college.

Having some play money can be wise — especially if it leaves you less tempted to make changes elsewhere, allowing compounding to work its magic over time.

Ron Lieber contributed reporting.

item.title: Anthropic’s I.P.O. Turns Tech Researchers Into Overnight Millionaires
item.description:
When Christopher Kirchoff, a former Pentagon official, joined Anthropic for a three-month fellowship in 2024, he was surrounded in the corporate lunchroom by “bookish” young technology workers who peppered him with questions about national security, he said.

The company only had hundreds of employees at the time, and he said he was awed by what people posted in internal Slack channels about what they were working on. He remembered one employee showing colleagues an early demonstration of artificial intelligence performing basic computer tasks, including buying a Nike sweatshirt online and shipping it to Anthropic’s office without human intervention. “Everyone knew it was a door to the future,” Mr. Kirchoff said.

That relatively small circle of workers is now in line for enormous paydays.

On Thursday, Anthropic vaulted into one of the world’s most valuable companies, after its record-setting initial public offering. That has created sudden, enormous wealth for hundreds of employees who had an early hand in its assent.

The bulk of the wealth the company created during its rise will go to a relatively small group of people, who joined it in the early years when Anthropic was worth far less. Anthropic’s investor prospectus ahead of the I.P.O. not only reflected how rapidly it has grown — it had 940 employees at the end of 2024 and about 5,300 as of September — but also showed that those 940 employees stood to gain the most.

It is unclear just how wealthy many of these employees have become, but Anthropic’s prospectus provides some idea of what employees who joined just two years ago would have coming their way. An employee awarded options on $1 million of stock in 2024 would now, on average, be sitting on about $66 million of stock once it vests, according to a New York Times analysis of the prospectus. Employees who joined earlier would be worth more. But even people who started a year ago might find themselves millionaires on paper now.

The company started trading on Nasdaq on Thursday, following what was the largest I.P.O. in history that valued Anthropic at about $1.5 trillion less than six years after its founding. Its shares opened notably higher than the $83 a share level set in its I.P.O., briefly pushing the company’s value over $2 trillion.

It reached that value more quickly than other tech companies. Anthropic’s crossing of the $1 trillion mark was more than a decade faster than it took other tech titans, including Meta, Google and SpaceX.

Many of the I.P.O.’s biggest winners are the kinds of employees Anthropic has said were a priority to hire in its early days: technically savvy engineers and scientists who believed in the race to rapidly — and responsibly — develop A.I. in the near future.

Anthropic’s founders have encouraged them to donate a portion of their stakes to charity, with the company matching the shares that employees pledged. Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, said last week on the company’s investor road show that a key to its success was focusing on hiring people who were “oriented toward the public benefit” rather than “jerks.”

“We’ve been very disciplined about turning down people who are deeply technically talented but don’t fit our culture,” he said. Dr. Amodei and his six co-founders, who made an emotional split from OpenAI during the pandemic in 2020, each own Anthropic stakes now worth more than $20 billion.

Employees who joined in 2024 might have had little reason, from the outside, to imagine how big the company would become. It had generated only about $41 million in sales the previous year and hadn’t yet attracted many brand-name venture capital investors to give their seal of approval.

As Anthropic has grown, it has actively sought out employees with more typical tech backgrounds and business-focused ambitions. The company wrote in its prospectus, for instance, that it planned to hire more sales people.

Many early employees have grown increasingly alarmed about the potential havoc that advanced A.I. could cause as companies like Anthropic continue to develop it. Some signed an online petition in July urging the U.S. government to lead an effort that would “pace” A.I. development to ensure proper safeguards are in place.

Nicholas Joseph, an early employee responsible for training Anthropic’s model, pointed out in the petition that work was being done by A.I. itself, rather than by humans. “I’m not sure if or where it tops out, but a rapid acceleration in capabilities might be dangerous for society,” he wrote.

Driving those fears now is the same calculus that attracted early A.I. believers to Anthropic — that the technology was going to keep developing. Lillian Li, a tech investor at the Scottish fund manager Baillie Gifford, remembered meeting Anthropic executives for the first time in 2023. She had heard initially about the company’s potential from A.I. researcher friends, all of whom had a sense that “the next five years were going to look very different.”

“They were very earnest and sincere people that wanted to do good for the world and no one had taken seriously prior to that,” she said.

item.title: Judge Allows Trump’s $15 Billion Case Against The Times to Proceed
item.description:
A federal judge on Thursday said that President Trump’s $15 billion defamation lawsuit against The New York Times and the book publisher Penguin Random House could proceed, moving it a step closer to a potential trial.

The judge, Steven D. Merryday of the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida, denied the request from The Times and the book publisher to dismiss all of Mr. Trump’s lawsuit. He said Mr. Trump could continue to sue over seven statements that his lawyers say damaged his reputation as a successful businessman and undermined his candidacy in the 2024 presidential election.

One of the statements was published in an October 2024 article in The Times and six were from a book published by Penguin Random House.

Judge Merryday wrote that Mr. Trump had plausibly argued that the seven statements, which centered on accusations that Mr. Trump had perpetrated or benefited from crimes like tax evasion or money laundering, were “based on incomplete, minimal information.”

At the same time, Judge Merryday dismissed many other parts of Mr. Trump’s lawsuit, saying that 27 of the statements Mr. Trump had highlighted as defamatory did not reach the high bar required by a public official to prove defamation. All of the statements in a September 2024 article from The Times were thrown out, along with multiple other statements in the book and in the October 2024 article.

Mr. Trump initially sued The Times and Penguin Random House in September 2025. The named defendants include The Times reporters Susanne Craig, Russ Buettner and Peter Baker; Ms. Craig and Mr. Buettner wrote the book in the case, “Lucky Loser.” The lawsuit, which was originally dismissed as unnecessarily lengthy and digressive, was refiled in October 2025.

Lawyers for The Times and Penguin Random House had defended the accuracy of the reporting and said in their argument for the lawsuit to be dismissed that Mr. Trump had not shown that the reporters had acted with “actual malice,” a legal standard meaning they had knowingly published something false or with reckless disregard as to its truth.

“The Times is encouraged to see Judge Merryday’s dismissal of almost all claims against us,” Charlie Stadtlander, a spokesman for The Times, said in a statement. “We continue to believe the remaining claim in the filing has no legal merit. We look forward to making this argument as we continue to defend ourselves against this baseless attack on The Times and the rights of the free and independent press in this country.”

A Penguin Random House spokeswoman, Claire Von Schilling, also welcomed the dismissal of most of the case, but said the publisher was disappointed that the judge did not dismiss “several statements that have been widely reported for years and never challenged by President Trump, even in prior litigation.”

“We are confident that the evidence in this case will lead to a full dismissal and continue to stand by the book and its authors,” she said.

Mr. Trump has frequently in his second term turned to litigation as a cudgel against the news media. A $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal was dismissed in October with prejudice, meaning Mr. Trump cannot refile it, though Mr. Trump has appealed the decision. A federal judge this month allowed a separate lawsuit from Mr. Trump against the BBC to proceed.Mr. Trump previously sued The Times in 2021 over a series of articles investigating his finances. That lawsuit was dismissed.

item.title: Stocks Often Prosper After an Abrupt C.E.O. Exit. Is Nvidia Different?
item.description:
Nvidia shareholders have lost so much money that the sum is practically unfathomable: around $2 trillion from late October through Thursday. Only Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon — and, for a brief time on Thursday, Anthropic — are even worth that much.

Nvidia’s vanished stock market value was roughly equivalent, in dollar terms, to simultaneously wiping three corporate giants, like JPMorgan, Exxon Mobil and United Health Care, off the face of the earth.

Not all of this colossal loss of wealth can be attributed to the forced departure of Jensen Huang, the Nvidia co-founder. But, undoubtedly, a great deal of Nvidia’s stock market plight stems from his unceremonious exit.

No wonder a swelling group of Nvidia loyalists is agitating for his return to the company. Mr. Huang said on Tuesday that he would be “honored to answer these calls and return as C.E.O.,” but the company’s board quickly made it clear that it would not welcome him back. So I wouldn’t count on Mr. Huang’s imminent return.

Yet this needn’t be a continuing calamity for Nvidia’s stock. History suggests that no executive at a mature company is irreplaceable, even if he is a global celebrity and a firm founder. After the initial shock and once a permanent replacement is in place, many companies recover in the stock market, several studies show.

Every company is different, however. The role of Mr. Huang at Nvidia poses special problems in assessing the company’s chances of prospering without him.

It’s not merely that he occupied a central position in what has arguably been the most important company in the most important industry in the world economy. Mr. Huang was also a pivotal player in U.S.-Chinese corporate relations, and the extent of his involvement in the supply of Nvidia chips and computing power to companies based in China isn’t yet known.

“Nvidia’s sales to China could be worth 20 percent or 30 percent” of the company’s peak stock market value, Aswath Damodaran, a New York University finance professor, said in an interview. That’s a big caveat, he said. It could be an exception to the rule that a stock like Nvidia ought to be solid enough to recover fully after a change in leadership.

Without Mr. Huang’s China connections, and amid national security concerns, investigations, congressional hearings and a harsher regulatory climate, “it may already be too late to restore all the lost value” coming from Nvidia’s sales, direct and indirect, to China, he said.

While much remains to be discovered, the basics of the Nvidia story are widely known. It designs advanced chips that power artificial intelligence, which made it an earnings machine, producing astonishing profits that, until its recent debacle, buoyed the entire stock market.

The company also served as a kind of central bank for the A.I. industry, pumping hundreds of billions of dollars into aspiring competitors, suppliers and customers, as my colleagues, Maureen Farrell and Rob Copeland, have written. For example, it committed to invest $10 billion in Anthropic before that A.I. giant’s initial public offering this week.

Nvidia remains a financial powerhouse — with revenue of $115.8 billion and profit of $65.3 billion in the three months through October, according to its latest disclosures on Tuesday. Both figures exceeded Wall Street’s expectations, and Nvidia projected revenue in the current quarter to be even larger, about $130 billion. Its longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, has been running the company on an interim basis since Nov. 12. That’s when Mr. Huang resigned.

He stepped down in the wake of a New York Times report that he had an affair with an employee at Nvidia, as well as with Alice Huang, a businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence has determined is an asset for Chinese intelligence. On Monday, the Trump administration moved to block the sale of advanced chips to data centers of the type run by Ms. Huang. She started a Singapore company called Megaspeed that is under investigation over allegations of smuggling chips to China. Chinese officials have denied that Ms. Huang is a spy for China. In his public comments in China, President Trump played down the episode.

The vast literature on the stock market effects of abrupt C.E.O. departures fails to offer many definitive lessons.

One thing that is clear, however, is that hasty executive exits tend to upset the stock market over short periods. One study of 30 such cases by BCA Research, an independent financial research firm, found that over the last three decades, 70 percent of the companies underperformed their benchmark significantlyover the following month.

In a separate study, Bespoke Investment Group, another independent research firm, examined how stocks performed one year after the chief executives were pushed out by their boards. It examined 30 cases that occurred within the last 10 years and found that, on average, the companies’ shares were down 12 percent one year later.

There was a silver lining in the Bespoke study. Of the six companies in the group in which the chief executives had to leave for what Bespoke called “bad behavior” involving “an inappropriate personal relationship,” their average stock was up 12 percent.

In an interview, Paul Hickey, a co-founder of Bespoke, called those returns “somewhat positive but not dramatic, because the market in that period was positive.” In fact, the S&P 500 over the last 10 years gained an annualized 13 percent, according to FactSet.

Yet another study, by Commons Capital, a wealth management firm, focused on 15 corporate founders who left their companies for a variety of reasons since 1985. It found that although the stock shares of most companies declined in the 12 months after a C.E.O. departure, a few well-known companies prospered.

Perhaps the most prominent was Apple, whose top executive, Steve Jobs, departed twice: in 1985, when he was pushed out by the Apple board; and in 2011, when he resigned because of the pancreatic cancer that led to his death. Both times, Apple stock soared over the following 12 months. But Mr. Jobs’s first successor, John Sculley, was himself forced out in 1993 when the company’s fortunes were ebbing. The second coming of Mr. Jobs culminated in the creation of the iPhone, the sleek gadget that transformed the world and turned around Apple’s fortunes. Mr. Jobs’s second successor, Tim Cook, never pretended to be the creative maestro that Mr. Jobs was, but Mr. Cook led Apple to tremendous gains, as an efficient and mature company, until resigning as chief executive and becoming chairman this year.

I ran the numbers on FactSet: From Aug. 24, 2011, when Mr. Cook became chief executive, until April 20, 2026, when he announced his resignation, Apple shares returned 24.3 percent, annualized, including dividends, compared with 15.2 percent for the S&P 500.

Nvidia, at this stage, seems to be “a fairly mature company with a good pipeline of products and a deep bench,” Mr. Damodaran said. “It could well resemble Apple under Tim Cook,” if not for the issues with China and the turbulence of the A.I. industry itself.

So what should one conclude from all this? Predicting how Nvidia will fare is a hazardous task. Whether Nvidia shares soar once again will depend on very specific issues that I won’t even try to assess in advance.

As an investor, I don’t even attempt to judge individual securities. Instead, I hold a part of the entire stock and bond markets through low-cost index funds and try to prosper over long periods when the economy does. What’s happened to Nvidia shares over the last month only reinforces the case.

Nvidia was the biggest company in the stock market until recently, and its decline is dragging down broad index returns. But at least these losses are being buffered by other stocks and bonds.

The future of A.I. and of the stock market won’t depend on just one company — not on Nvidia and probably not on Anthropic, which began trading shares to the public on Thursday. But Anthropic warned in its prospectus that its A.I. has the potential to destroy humanity.

Even well-diversified investors have plenty to worry about.

item.title: Anthropic’s Banner Debut Not Enough to Stop Slide in Stock Market
item.description:
The blockbuster market debut for Anthropic, one of the biggest players in artificial intelligence, was not enough to turn the broader tide for stocks, with major indexes slumping at the end of another tumultuous week for investors.

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq benchmarks were on course for their worst weeks in well over a year, dragged down by technology stocks as traders question the durability of the A.I. boom.

The S&P 500 has fallen over 5 percent through Thursday, the worst week for the index since April 2025, when the market convulsed in response to the announcement of President Trump’s sweeping global tariffs. Futures markets suggested that stocks would continue to slide when U.S. trading opens on Friday.

Anthropic’s stock, after surging by double-digit percentages in its trading debut on Thursday, itself slipped 8 percent premarket.

Notes: Data is delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

The declines have persisted despite generally favorable reactions from analysts and investors to the week’s major events, billed ahead of time as pivotal to the A.I. trade that has powered the market for months but has faltered more recently.

Nvidia’s earnings report on Tuesday helped to calm fears of a slowdown in growth of the A.I. build-out, with the giant chip maker raising its profit forecast. It was a brief respite for the company, which is reeling after the resignation of its larger-than-life chief executive, Jensen Huang, following revelations that he had two affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence officials determined was feeding information to Beijing.

Then on Thursday, Anthropic jumped more than 17 percent in its first day of trading, achieving a trillion-dollar valuation after setting a record for the largest public offering in history. Robust demand for the shares of the maker of the Claude chatbot suggested that investors were still optimistic about aspects of the A.I. industry.

But the rest of the market has continued to slide. The S&P 500 has fallen for six straight trading days, its longest losing streak since April 2024. Every sector of the index is lower for the week, led by tech shares. The Nasdaq Composite is on course for a loss of 5 percent this week.

Notes: Data is delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

“Unfortunately, there isn’t an obvious catalyst or event to improve sentiment as we head into year-end,” said Stuart Kaiser, an analyst at Citi, adding that “there are no clear signposts to swing the pendulum.”

Traders tend to book profits in the run-up to Thanksgiving, mindful that markets slow into the end of the year, which can make it harder to move in and out of positions. There is also typically trepidation around this time about holding large positions through year’s end.

Nvidia has fallen nearly 40 percent since the S&P 500 peaked in early October, accounting for roughly half of the 8 percent drop in the index over that period, according to Adam Turnquist, chief technical strategist for LPL Financial. Nvidia has been “the big factor” weighing on the market, he said, emblematic of “the broader fear over an A.I. slowdown.” The chip maker’s stock was down, again, in premarket trading on Friday.

Chip makers and related stocks were also weighed down by a report released on Thursday by Hunterbrook, a short-selling firm that profits from bets against companies, that claimed Advanced Micro Devices had supplied U.S.-blacklisted Chinese companies with updates to keep its chips running. (AMD said that the claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships.”)

Anthropic’s newly listed stock soared as much as 38 percent in early trading on Thursday, but as the day progressed, the air came out of the company’s ballooning price. Its shares ended the day up 17 percent, at $97 a share.

That’s still a healthy rise from its I.P.O. price of $83 per share, but suggested a more restrained optimism for the company’s prospects than the initial flurry of trades.

Still, analyst recommendations for the Anthropic, collated by the market data firm FactSet, show bullish expectations for the future. Ben Reitzes at Melius Research represents the high-water mark, with an initial price target of $155 per share. At the other end of the spectrum is Patrick Walravens at Citizens, with a target of $125.

But the CBOE Vix Volatility index, a measure known as the market’s “fear gauge,” which measure investors’ expectations of volatility over the next 30 days, recently rose just above its peak in the whipsaw aftermath of the midterm elections, a sign of market jitters.

“There’s been a lot of talk about whether the A.I. trade had gotten ahead of itself,” said Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, who pointed to Nvidia’s strong earnings and the initial rise in Anthropic’s shares as “notable” signs for investors. “That doesn’t settle every valuation debate,” he added, “but it’s pretty strong affirmation that the market is not ready to walk away from the trade just yet.”

item.title: Can Anthropic Revive the A.I. Trade?
item.description:
Andrew here. At the DealBook Summit this week, my colleagues Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan led a remarkable panel on the midterms and what they mean for 2028.

The panelists included Stacey Abrams, David Axelrod, Alyssa Farah Griffin, Morris Katz, Dan Senor and David Urban — three Democrats and three Republicans, at least two of whom have worked for President Trump. What made it fascinating was how little anyone held back. It was an unfiltered look at how campaigns are quietly strategizing for the next cycle — and yes, at times it got heated. You can watch it here.

Anthropic just pulled off the biggest I.P.O. ever and minted billions in paper profits for its founders, employees and pre-offering backers. Yet investors seem to want more.

Shares in the artificial intelligence giant are down about 9 percent in premarket trading, and S&P 500 futures are in the red. It’s a sign that there are still significant hurdles for Anthropic and for the broader A.I. industry.

By the numbers:

Anthropic now has a market value of about $1.27 trillion — or, on a fully diluted stock basis, nearly $1.8 trillion.

The company raised about $120 billion from the I.P.O.

Anthropic’s offering minted huge winners, beyond its seven founders:

Even recently hired employees enjoyed windfalls: A staff member awarded options on $1 million of stock in 2024 would now, on average, be sitting on about $66 million of stock when it vests, The Times calculates. (Unlike most I.P.O.s, employees were able to start selling their holdings right away.)

The lead underwriters, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, are set to collect about $113 million each from the offering.

Anthropic’s venture capital backers are set to receive generational returns: Spark Capital, the only investment firm with a seat on the company’s board, invested $75 million in the company in 2023 — and now sits on a stake valued at $17.1 billion.

Others sitting on windfalls include the hedge fund billionaire Gregory Jensen and the tech mogul Dustin Moskovitz (who told The Times that he’s worried about A.I. safety and won’t personally profit from selling Anthropic shares in the open market.)

Ravi Mhatre, a founder of Lightspeed Venture Partners and a major investor in the company, told DealBook’s Michael de la Merced, “Anthropic as a public company creates more of an understanding with the public markets that there is a viable business model.”

Yet Anthropic’s I.P.O. hasn’t totally allayed investor fears about the A.I. boom. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.2 percent yesterday, as the offering failed to reignite confidence in A.I. stocks, which have slumped amid concerns about valuations, spending and the turmoil at Nvidia.

(It didn’t help that shares in the chip maker AMD tanked yesterday after the short seller Hunterbrook accused the company of supplying U.S.-blacklisted Chinese companies with processors. AMD has disputed the report.)

Anthropic still faces headwinds, including the $900 billion it’s projected to spend on data centers and computing power in the next several years. And while its A.I. models are considered among the most advanced, it faces competition from almost-as-capable open-weight models that cost far less to use.

That raises questions about what lies ahead for OpenAI, Anthropic’s biggest rival, which is set to go public next year.

Chipmakers face scrutiny over their China links. California’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, has opened an investigation into whether Nvidia’s advanced chips or their trade secrets have been transferred to China. But in a sign of how complicated it might be to police the sector, lawmakers in Washington disclosed that the Commerce Department had approved sales of more than 800,000 artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies, some with military ties.

The White House replaces its top cybersecurity official. The official, Sean Cairncross, left his position as national cyber director days after a series of technological outages grounded commercial air traffic in the U.S., and disrupted banking and email services. Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon’s chief information officer, will replace him.

A regulator rebukes companies tied to Mark Walter. The Delaware Department of Insurance said that two insurance firms controlled by Walter, the billionaire owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers, had misled it and other regulators about billions of dollars in assets they held that were investments in other businesses tied to him. Separately, Walter is nearing a deal to sell the Los Angeles Sparks of the WNBA for $750 million, Sportico reports, citing unnamed sources.

Grand Theft Auto VI pops off. Take-Two Interactive’s update to the action-adventure video game franchise has posted Hollywood blockbuster-like numbers, selling a reported 24.6 million copies for over $2.3 billion in its first two days. Consider: It takes up to an estimated 100 hours to complete G.T.A. VI, the “Super Bowl of video games,” which is a sort of crime simulator and cartoonish sendup of American life set in a sexy, neon stand-in for Miami. That has left schools and businesses bracing for absences with so-called G.T.A. flu.

Anthropic was seemingly everywhere in midtown Manhattan yesterday. The company’s black-and-white logo and its advertising tagline — “What we make of this moment, will make this moment” — blanketed billboard after eye-popping billboard in Times Square.

A few blocks up, Morgan Stanley and Barclays, two banks that helped Anthropic go public, wrapped their buildings in giant scrolling text, celebrating the record-breaking I.P.O.

The splashy party drew throngs of TV crews, some A.I. protesters and plenty of gawkers. On the corner of Broadway and 46th Street, one confused man asked DealBook’s Bernhard Warner, “What are they selling, anyhow?”

At Broadway and 43rd Street, the message became clearer: Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s C.E.O., appeared on a screen several stories high outside the Nasdaq MarketSite headquarters, talking up the potential of Claude, Anthropic’s chatbot, and warning of A.I.’s wider risks.

The charitable foundation run jointly by the embattled former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori, is a potentially significant asset if their marriage goes sideways.

Already one of the country’s largest private charities, it has grown much bigger recently, Theodore Schleifer reports for DealBook.

The foundation has nearly $13 billion in assets, according to a tax return from 2025 obtained by The New York Times. Its assets surged by about 40 percent that year.

The Huangs are co-presidents of the entity, called the Jen-hsun & Lori Huang Foundation.

It’s not known if the couple plans to divorce. But the state of their 41-year marriage has been the subject of speculation ever since Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful.

Huang resigned as C.E.O. of Nvidia last week after reports of his affairs with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese asset, as well as an executive at his company. At the DealBook Summit on Wednesday, tech leaders expressed empathy for Huang.

A split would be costly for Huang. His net worth currently stands at $122 billion, according to Bloomberg. High-profile divorces of several tech founders have created a class of female billionaire philanthropists, including MacKenzie Scott and Melinda French Gates.

Most of the Huang Foundation’s spending in 2025 went to an Nvidia partner. The foundation disclosed in its tax filing that it prepaid for $350 million in computing power that it is in the process of awarding to nonprofits.

That compute was purchased from CoreWeave, which Nvidia previously disclosed had sold $108.3 million of computing capacity to the Huang’s foundation.

In the A.I. race between the U.S. and China, much of the focus has been on access to advanced computer chips. For example, the Trump administration said on Monday it would close a loophole that allowed workarounds for Chinese companies to access Nvidia’s semiconductors.

But increasingly, there’s another factor that threatens to throttle the growth of Chinese tech companies: Money.

China can’t keep pace with U.S. capital markets, Sui-Lee Wee and Li You report for The Times:

Venture capital investment in China lags far behind that of the United States. Alibaba, Baidu, and Tencent, three tech giants backing some of China’s leading A.I. companies, are grappling with negative cash flows. And investor enthusiasm for A.I. has soured. Since the end of July, China’s STAR 50 index, its version of the Nasdaq, has plunged 43 percent in a deeper sell-off than the recent downturn in American tech stocks.

China’s biggest tech companies are expected to double capital spending this year to $139 billion, even though the revenue from their A.I. labs covers less than 8 percent of that amount, according to Rhodium Group, a research firm. It forecasts that spending could top $193 billion in 2027.

Part of the challenge is the business model. Many Chinese companies have embraced open source A.I., which means that when they charge for access, they may soon see competitors offer the same model at a lower price.

China’s six leading A.I. firms together generate about one-tenth the combined revenue of OpenAI and Anthropic, according to Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization.

The cost of compute is rising with U.S. chip restrictions. “We simply can’t afford to train the largest models available right now,” Liang Wenfeng, C.E.O. of DeepSeek, recently told investors, according to a leaked transcript of the call.

Deals

Intuit agreed to sell Mailchimp, an email marketing company it bought in 2021 for $12 billion, to Bending Spoons, an Italian acquirer of older tech businesses, for about $3.7 billion. (CNBC)

Sanofi is reportedly weighing a takeover bid for Insmed, a U.S. maker of treatments for respiratory diseases, with a market value of $31.6 billion. (Bloomberg)

“Lenders Aim to Bar SpaceX from Launching $40bn of Chips Into Orbit” (FT)

Politics, policy and regulation

The Senate passed a bill to speed up the federal permitting process for energy projects and to require data centers to pay for the energy they use, which could double by 2030. (NYT, CNBC)

Investment accounts tied to President Trump bought shares in companies that recently scored federal contracts or that grew closer to the White House. (CNBC)

Law firms that gave the White House free legal work are preparing for inquiries by congressional Democrats. (FT)

Best of the rest

Americans have access to ever more powerful technology, but many are feeling increasingly powerless. (NYT)

The two chairmen of the white-shoe law firm Sullivan & Cromwell, including Robert Giuffra, one of Trump’s personal lawyers, plan to step down in 2028. (WSJ)

“That ‘SNL’ Sister Sketch: It’s More Like Nonfiction” (NYT)

item.title: Savings Bonds Offer Enticing Rates. You Need to Prove Your Identity First.
item.description:
Newly issued government savings bonds that guard against inflation are currently paying 5.51 percent interest rates, far better than the highest rate available on federally insured savings accounts.

But since Oct. 28, the Treasury Department has required that customers use a private service, ID.me, to verify their identities. Until they do so, customers can’t get access to the federal TreasuryDirect website to buy bonds or see their holdings online.

Not everyone is thrilled about the new procedure.

John Ferreira, a retiree and Treasury Direct user in Kensington, Calif., said he received an email from the site in late October, telling him to create an account within a week with ID.me to access his holdings, including I bonds and a two-year Treasury note. He had been logging on infrequently, he said, with a username, password and an account number. Sometimes, he was asked to answer a few security questions.

Mr. Ferreira, 81, said he found the email suspicious, because warnings to take swift action on money matters are considered “a tell-tale sign” of financial fraud. He said he wondered: “Is it a scam?” Although the email proved legitimate, Mr. Ferreira said he still objected to having TreasuryDirect “hold my bonds hostage unless I used a third-party app.”

In a statement, Wes Turbeville, a company senior vice president, said: “We want every ID.me authentication to go smoothly and recognize that anything less can be frustrating, especially if the user is unfamiliar with online identity proofing processes.” He added that users also have the option to prove their identities using a “live, secure” video call on a computer and can reach support at help.id.me.

Here’s what to know if you are a TreasuryDirect customer or want to become one.

The TreasuryDirect website says ID.me offers a “faster, more secure experience” than its traditional, in-house log on system. Most users can verify their identities in under 10 minutes, TreasuryDirect says. Once they do so, logging on takes just seconds for subsequent visits.

A Treasury spokeswoman, Athina Lawson, said in an email that ID.me is a federally certified identity verification provider and that the change “provides additional safeguards to protect customers’ personal and financial information and reduce the risk of unauthorized account access.”

ID.me was founded in 2010 by an Army veteran, Blake Hall, who saw another veteran hand over his discharge paperwork to a store employee to claim a military discount, according to its website. Mr. Hall thought there should be a better way for people to prove their identities without disclosing personal information, according to its website. The company now offers identity verification services for about two dozen federal websites as well as to many state government agencies and private businesses to confirm that online users are who they say they are and prevent fraud.

For many federal websites, including Social Security, Medicare and Veterans Affairs, ID.me is often offered as an option alongside Login.gov, a government-administered online identity verification service.

In the case of TreasuryDirect, however, ID.me is the sole option available. Ms. Lawson, the Treasury Department spokeswoman, said the department was also evaluating using Login.gov.

The Internal Revenue Service, which is part of Treasury, added Login.gov as an option in addition to ID.me for its websites a few weeks ago, an I.R.S. spokesman said.

To use ID.me, users need government identification like a driver’s license or passport, their Social Security number and, typically, a smartphone with a camera. You may be asked for photo verification using your cellphone, the Treasury Direct website says, so the service can confirm the user is the same person shown on the ID.

Users who don’t have smartphones may need extra time to complete verification. Jonathan Kahn, 70, of New York City, said he uses a so-called VoIP line, which connects voice calls over the internet, but which turned out to be incompatible with ID.me. It took several hours, including time waiting for two online help sessions, before the issue was identified, he said; eventually, he was authorized using an alternative method.

Users can contact ID.me for online help if they have trouble.

Some privacy groups have raised concerns about the service’s data retention policies. ID.me’s website said it may retain biometric data, such as “facial geometry recognition,” for as little as 24 hours or as long as three years, depending on the department using the service. The timing can also vary depending on the requirements of the first agency a customer uses to verify their identity with the service.

According to TreasuryDirect’s website, ID.me acts “solely as an identity provider,” and neither TreasuryDirect nor ID.me “sells, rents, or shares your personal information” for marketing or advertising purposes.

Two senators, Ron Wyden of Oregon and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, both Democrats, raised concerns about the move to ID.me in a letter on Oct. 27 to top Treasury and I.R.S. officials. They said that the transition was “needlessly rushed” and that savings bonds are primarily held by older Americans, “who may lack the digital proficiency to quickly transition between complicated online systems.” They also said the rationale for expanded use of ID.me was “unclear,” asserting that Login.gov meets necessary security standards.

Ms. Lawson said TreasuryDirect began notifying customers of the change on Aug. 3, using email, the TreasuryDirect website, and messages displayed when users logged on, before beginning the transition to ID.me on Sept. 13. The site also published answers to frequently asked questions on its website.

The senators had asked that the switch be delayed until after the 2027 tax filing season so that users could continue to use their old log on to obtain tax documents, such as interest statements for bonds redeemed this year.

TreasuryDirect says ID.me offers the “simplest” way to get tax documents like 1099-INT forms showing interest paid, but users can also ask to have the forms mailed by calling TreasuryDirect’s customer support at 844-284-2676.

Rates on series I savings bonds, known as I bonds, can change every six months based on inflation. New I bonds are paying 5.51 percent through April 30, 2027.

In comparison, the highest rate available on high-yield, federally insured savings accounts is just over 4 percent, according to Bankrate.

The rate on I bonds is a combination of a fixed rate, set when the bond is issued and lasting for the bond’s 30-year life, and a variable rate that changes every six months — on May 1 and Nov. 1 — based on the Consumer Price Index. The variable rate applies to new bonds as well as to older bonds that are still earning interest.

Individuals can buy $10,000 in I bonds per year. (The option to buy an extra $5,000 in bonds with your tax refund was eliminated last year).

You can’t redeem the bonds for at least one year. And if you cash them in before five years, there’s a penalty — you’ll forfeit the last three months’ worth of interest.

Interest earned on I bonds is exempt from state and local income taxes but is subject to federal tax, although you can wait to pay until you cash in the bonds.

You don’t have to use the TreasuryDirect website to manage paper bonds. You can ask your bank if it will cash them, or you can fill out a form and mail them to the Treasury Department.

item.description:
I am a New York Times reporter covering white-collar workers and the ways that new technologies and economic trends affect their work lives.

As companies adopt artificial intelligence, they are giving employees sometimes contradictory instructions for how to use it. This year, many tech companies encouraged employees to maximize their A.I. use, only to turn around and ask employees to become more discriminating in their use of the technology a few months later.

If you work outside a tech company and have been encouraged to use A.I., I’d like to hear from you. I’d like to know whether your marching orders on using A.I. have changed — and, if so, how.

item.title: Inside Tribal Leaders’ Fight to Ban Kalshi
item.description:
James Siva, the leader of the California Nations Indian Gaming Association, called a meeting to order last month to discuss prediction markets, which many tribes see as an existential threat to their livelihoods.

For decades, tribes have relied heavily on casino gaming revenue to provide social services and fund their governments. But Kalshi — a prediction market that allows users to bet on almost anything — has been encroaching on their business, they said. Eight tribes sued the company over the past 18 months to ban it from operating on their lands, citing laws that grant them sovereignty to decide what — if any — gaming should be permitted.

In a windowless convention room at the Hard Rock Hotel and Casino Sacramento, lawyers for some of the association’s 62 tribes gave updates on various legal challenges — calling the outcomes “mostly favorable.” As sounds from the casino floor bled through the door, a lawyer for Blue Lake Rancheria, a tribe which recently won an injunction against Kalshi, said it was time for action.

“We’re going after their pocketbooks,” said Lester Marston, a Cahuilla Indian who has represented tribes for more than 40 years. “The tribes can get their lost revenue back by enforcing their laws.”

Mr. Siva agreed. “This is absolutely the biggest threat we’ve seen in a long time, perhaps ever,” he said.

Native American tribes are part of an escalating battle in the United States over the legality of prediction markets, a question of whether they are defined as online casinos or financial tools. Dozens of tribes — long battered by displacement and shifting federal policies — say the answer is a matter of survival, and that they must retain control over the gaming industry on their lands.

The companies and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates the markets at the federal level, have said that they are financial trading tools. But some states and tribes have argued that the markets are no different than sports gambling, which they regulate under existing laws.

Around two dozen states are in legal battles with Kalshi over enforcing their own anti-gambling laws and blocking the app from operating in their states, often citing potential harms to tribes. In some cases, state attorneys general have made the argument that Kalshi and other prediction markets should be banned altogether.

Judges have issued mixed decisions in the lawsuits, and the cases are expected to eventually reach the Supreme Court. To hurry that decision, a coalition of 145 tribes wrote a letter last month asking the Supreme Court to address whether prediction market platforms can offer sports betting outside established federal, state and tribal gaming laws.

Tribes have long been granted the authority to govern themselves, legal experts said.

“Funding support is evaporating,” said Ethan Jones, a lawyer at Galanda Broadman in Seattle who specializes in federal Indian law. “That’s putting more and more pressure on the tribes to come up with their own revenue to support these essential governmental services — providing basic necessities, clean water, housing for their people.”

“And it all comes to gaming,” he said.

Kalshi says it does not take business from tribes. Their casinos offer a destination and hospitality experience, the company said, while prediction markets allow people to trade on future events.

Some tribes have also decided to join them. Five tribes have announced partnerships with Kalshi in recent weeks to offer their own prediction market apps following permission granted by the C.F.T.C. Leaders for the tribes that teamed up with the company said they did not view prediction markets as a threat to tribal gaming, but as a promising economic lever.

“Economic development is very core to them, and it’s not always easy to come by,” Max Crowley, the vice president for business development at Kalshi, said about the tribes. “Getting to a few thousand active users on these apps will turn into something significant.”

Overall, gaming isn’t in decline, he said. Either way, the tribes who are partnering with Kalshi are “launching financial apps,” Mr. Crowley said, “not launching gaming apps.”

Mr. Siva, 42, belongs to the Morongo Band of Mission Indians, which has a reservation in Southern California between Banning and Cabazon. In 1983, a year before he was born, the tribe was one of the first in the nation to open a bingo hall to generate revenue and provide employment during Reagan administration-era funding cuts to Native Americans.

Local and state authorities threatened to prosecute. The tribe joined with a neighboring reservation to file a lawsuit against the Riverside County, defending their right to operate. Five years later, the Supreme Court ruled tribes had the right to conduct gambling on their own lands, citing in part tribal sovereignty. The following year, Congress passed the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, mandating that revenue from tribal gaming must support social services.

Since then, tribal casino gambling has become a $46.2 billion industry. Nearly 250 Native American governments operate 545 gaming facilities across 29 states, according to the National Indian Gaming Commission’s latest report.

Enterprise Rancheria, the tribe that hosted the California Nations Indian Gaming Association meeting in October, broke ground on its casino in 2016. The result has been life changing, said its chairwoman, Glenda Nelson.

The casino has brought in “enough money that we are all starting to recover from the severe poverty of multiple generations,” Ms. Nelson, 66, said.

Tribal gaming has also faced setbacks. In 2018, the Supreme Court struck down a federal ban on state-authorized sports betting, setting off the nationwide legalization of sports gambling that upended tribal economies. Now, many fear the prediction markets may cause further strain.

Mr. Siva, who graduated from Columbia University with a degree in ethnic studies, is driven by his tribe’s legacy helping to establish tribal gaming. He became head of the California Nations Indian Gaming Association in 2018 and has since been repeatedly re-elected.

Mr. Siva first heard people were wagering on prediction markets during the 2024 presidential election. By the time his association met at a February conference the next year, he had grown concerned. The Morongo Band of Mission Indians grosses around several hundred million dollars from their casino each year, but they had begun to hear about customers using prediction market apps on their phones at the same time they were pulling slots.

Tribes and tribal organizations began having weekly meetings to discuss the markets. In April 2025, Mr. Siva and a handful of leaders from the Indian Gaming Association held a video call with executives at Kalshi.

Mr. Mansour, Kalshi’s chief executive, said the company was interested in partnerships. Mr. Siva explained the need to defend tribal sovereignty, and said he left feeling uneasy.

By that July, three tribes in California, including Blue Lake Rancheria and Chicken Ranch Rancheria of Me-Wuk Indians, filed a lawsuit against Kalshi.

It was the right move, Mr. Siva said. Tribes could lose around 5 percent of their annual gaming revenue to prediction markets, according to early projections compiled by a market research firm, KlasRobinson Q.E.D. (Kalshi disputes the findings of the report.)

For tribes, that means critical funding for essential services like health care, education and elder care. Mr. Siva feared it could push them “backwards in time.”

But the tribes faced setbacks in the lower courts. In November 2025, a Federal District Court in California denied the tribes’ request for a preliminary injunction to block Kalshi from offering sports event contracts on their lands. The tribes appealed the decision.

In May, responding to a lawsuit with similar allegations filed by the Ho-Chunk Nation of Wisconsin, a federal judge ruled that the tribe had “produced little evidence” that its casinos were losing customers to Kalshi and declined to issue a preliminary injunction.

Mr. Siva’s group stepped in, funding an economic impact study for the Ho-Chunk Nation. . About 5.6 percent of the tribe’s gaming revenue came from customers who also use Kalshi, according to the report, putting “revenue at risk.”

States were also filing lawsuits against Kalshi, citing in part tribal concerns. In Washington State, where casinos are allowed only on tribal lands, tribal leaders celebrated when a state judge ordered Kalshi to cease most operations in August.

Another win came in September, when the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit in San Francisco ruled in favor of the California tribes, leading to an order barring Kalshi’s sports contracts from their reservations. (The C.F.T.C. this month directed prediction markets to drop any geographic restrictions, saying that they must operate on a uniform national scale under federal financial regulations.)

Not all tribal gaming is equal. Nine percent of the largest facilities generate about 56 percent of the industry’s total gaming revenue. Smaller gaming facilities and those in rural areas will feel the economic impact of prediction markets first, Mr. Siva said.

That could be the case for Colorado River Indian Tribes, which has operated the BlueWater Resort and Casino in Parker, Ariz., for roughly three decades. The casino’s busy season starts this month, when snowbirds arrive in the state, and will likely be a test of whether prediction markets erode revenue, said Rebecca Loudbear, the attorney general for the tribe.

“Their marketing is heavy. You cannot get on TikTok and not have every other ad be for Kalshi,” she said. “A tribe doesn’t have that resource for marketing.”

Driving through the Morongo reservation in October, Mr. Siva pointed out a new health clinic tucked into the valley surrounded by brown mountains. Not far from the tribe’s original bingo hall, now a community center, a new school was under construction.

“Everything that we do for our members is all funded the majority through the casino,”he said.

In Mr. Siva’s lifetime, the tribe had pulled itself from financial hardship, going from operating a modest bingo hall to among the highest-grossing tribal gaming properties on the West Coast. He does not intend to watch it go.

“It’s not just the loss of tribal gaming revenue,” he said, “It’s a fundamental change in how gaming will exist in the United States. That’s what’s at risk for everybody here.”

item.title: Nissan Shuts Down System Used for Repairs After Hack Attempt
item.description:
The Japanese carmaker Nissan said that a cybersecurity incident has prompted it to shut down a system that allows repair shops to diagnose problems with vehicle electronics. Among other things, the shutdown prevents car dealers from making replacement key fobs for customers.

The shutdown comes after a series of computer system outages and problems at Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase and the Federal Aviation Administration. It provided another reminder of how vulnerable computer systems are and their capacity to disrupt daily life in unexpected ways.

Virtually all modern automobiles are equipped with computers and processors, which are known as electronic control units. These devices control brakes, steering, locks, the flow of fuel and air into the engine, and a variety of other functions.

Like any computer systems, they can be compromised or fail. “You are talking about a very complex piece of machinery with a lot of different entry points,” said Ari Lightman, a professor of digital media and marketing at Carnegie Mellon University.

“I can imagine we are going to hear more of this,” Mr. Lightman added, noting that artificial intelligence has given hackers new tools to find and exploit vulnerabilities.

Nissan said in a statement that it “identified unauthorized access to part of a vehicle diagnostic system used by our dealers globally.” The carmaker has “temporarily suspended the system while we conduct a detailed investigation.”

The company, which is based in Yokohama, Japan, said it could provide no further information on who might have tried to hack the system.

The shutdown means that service technicians cannot reprogram the electronic control units in Nissan and Infiniti vehicles manufactured since 1995, the company said in a notice to dealers and repair shops.

“It could affect people’s ability to get their car repaired and get back to work,” said Gang Wang, an associate professor of computer science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

Nissan said that “dealers remain open and can continue performing many service and repair activities.” But, the company added, “certain repairs that require access to the affected diagnostic system may be delayed.”

Among other things, the shutdown means that dealers may not be able to program replacement key fobs, a problem for anyone who has lost or damaged one.

Nissan began the shutdown on Nov. 13, according to a notice to dealers, which has not been widely reported. As of Friday, Nissan had not resolved the issue.

That is an unusually long shutdown, Professor Wang said. “Even an outage that last hours or a day — you consider that a very long outage,” he said.

Other automakers have also experienced hacks, some of them much more serious than the one Nissan is dealing with. Last year, hackers broke into the computer systems of Jaguar Land Rover, forcing the company, which is owned by India’s Tata Motors, to suspend production for five weeks.

item.title: Many Etsy Sellers Close Up Shop Over Site’s New A.I. Policy
item.description:
Many longtime owners of shops on Etsy, the online marketplace known for its handmade goods, said this week that they had left the site over a policy change that they said leaves them vulnerable to exploitation by artificial intelligence companies.

Language in Etsy’s new terms, set to take effect on Dec. 16, says the company and its “third party partners and vendors” reserve the right to use sellers’ content to “develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies.”

The terms say that Etsy and its partners will use such technologies in part to improve the platform and keep it safe for users. The previous version of the terms did not include a clause about using content for artificial intelligence.

“Etsy decided that selling on their platform now means letting them train AI on our artwork AND resell that data to third parties, with no way to opt out,” Aaron Millard, an illustrator, wrote in a Instagram post announcing that he was deleting the shop that he has run for nearly a decade. “My work took years to learn and create. I won’t let it be stolen.”

Kristen and Geoff Zephyrus, the founders of the home goods and stationary brand Cognitive Surplus, which has sold its products on Etsy for 13 years, also deleted their shop. In an Instagram post, they accused the company of claiming “perpetual, free, boundless permission to not only train AI on our art, but also to resell the data for profit.”

“For Etsy to be helping to train algorithms with our human content is just unimaginably awful,” Kristen Zephyrus said in an interview. “We don’t want anything to do with that.”

In a statement posted to Etsy’s website on Monday, James Ossman, the company’s vice president for customer operations, addressed the site’s sellers directly.

Etsy will not “use your content to train A.I. models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity,” Ossman wrote. He cited the development of fraud detection tools and advertisements on the site as among the reasons for granting third parties access to sellers’ content.

A representative for Etsy did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.

Many publicly traded internet companies like Etsy have been caught between pressure from shareholders to embrace artificial intelligence and the ire of users who reject the technology.

Big bets by major firms and their investors on the A.I. revolution have helped the U.S. stock market set records in recent years. But Americans in general are much less enthusiastic. A Gallup poll from the summer found that nearly 40 percent of Americans feel that A.I. does more harm than good. Many of the Democratic political candidates who swept into power during the midterm elections this month campaigned explicitly against A.I. companies and data centers.

Etsy, which was founded in 2005 to help independent artisans find customers online, is no stranger to user revolt. In 2022, more than 20,000 Etsy sellers went on strike to protest a 30 percent increase in its base-line sales fee, to 6.5 percent from 5 percent. In October, the company announced tighter restrictions on so-called A.I. slop after many users decried such content.

item.title: Grand Theft Auto VI Made $3.79 Billion in a Single Day
item.description:
Grand Theft Auto VI made $3.79 billion in sales in one day, the publisher Rockstar Games announced on Friday, with more than 32 million copies of the video game preordered.

The game, set in the alterna-Miami known as Vice City, benefited from 13 years of pent-up demand since the release of Grand Theft Auto V. It received rave reviews that credited the game with shootout thrills, matchless graphics, a detailed virtual universe and a surprisingly tender love story.

Rockstar, which is a subsidiary of Take-Two Interactive, said in a news release that it was “the biggest entertainment launch in history.”

In certain respects, it is difficult to argue. The figure of $3.79 billion would be the biggest global box office of any movie, besting the current top earner, “Avengers: Endgame,” by nearly $900 million. This year’s highest-grossing movie, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” has taken in $2.5 billion since its release four months ago. Its opening-weekend haul was $932 million.

Taylor Swift’s recent Eras Tour topped $2 billion in ticket sales after 149 dates spanning nearly two years, making it by far the best-selling concert tour ever.

Grand Theft Auto VI’s price point — $79.99 for the standard edition and $99.99 for an enhanced version — means that more people purchased tickets to see “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and other top-grossing films.

But Grand Theft Auto VI is expected to continue selling robustly through the holiday season, and even more when it becomes available on computers. Currently it can be played on the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S consoles. Its predecessor, Grand Theft Auto V, sold more than 30 million copies in its first months and an additional 200 million in the following years.

Whenever the online version of the game debuts, players will also begin spending money to purchase in-game cash that can be used to buy things — outfits, cars, nightclubs — within the Vice City universe. Wedbush Securities estimates that Rockstar will generate $1.2 billion in annual sales from Grand Theft Auto Online once the latest version is available.

item.title: Nvidia Said to Face S.E.C. Probe Into Its Accounting Practices
item.description:
The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia’s accounting practices, according to two people briefed on the matter, adding to the mounting scrutiny facing the embattled technology giant.

It is not clear whether the investigation is related to the revelations that Nvidia’s former chief executive, Jensen Huang, had an affair with Alice Huang, the executive who U.S. intelligence has concluded was a Chinese asset.

The investigation is in its early stages, said another person briefed on the matter. The people spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a confidential government inquiry. And it is possible that no civil charges will come from it.

Questions around accounting have surfaced amid reporting about Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed, a Singaporean based company where Ms. Huang was an executive.

Officials at the Commerce Department had been investigating whether Megaspeed smuggled Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips into China in violation of American export restrictions. After The New York Times reported on Megaspeed and Mr. Huang’s close relationship with Ms. Huang last October, Nvidia changed how it reported its sales geographically. Singapore vanished from its financial disclosures as it started reporting sales based on “customers’ headquarters” rather than “billing location.”

Megaspeed has said that it complies with all laws and that Ms. Huang currently has no role in the company. She has not returned requests for comment, and the Chinese government has dismissed the spying claims.

A Nvidia spokesman did not respond to requests for comment.

The Wall Street Journal and Reuters earlier reported the existence of an S.E.C. inquiry.

The company remains under pressure from investors, with shares closing down 14 percent on Friday and a little more than 21 percent over the past week.

Mr. Huang resigned from the company earlier this month. Nvidia appointed the chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as its temporary chief executive, while it looks for an executive to permanently fill the role. Nvidia’s board has hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead an investigation into the circumstances that led to Mr. Huang’s resignation.

Following Mr. Huang’s departure, he has received a swell of support from many technology executives, as well as President Trump. “He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person” Mr. Trump said Friday. “I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back.”

The chair of Nvidia’s board, Harvey C. Jones, said earlier this week that the “the Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.” He added that Mr. Huang had exhibited “personal behavior inconsistent with its code of conduct, standards and cultural norms.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday he wanted more information about Nvidia’s internal workings.

“I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia,” Mr. Bessent said. “Were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?”

item.title: Judge Approves $7 Billion Settlement Over Claims That Roundup Caused Cancer
item.description:
A Missouri state court gave final approval on Friday to a $7.25 billion nationwide settlement that will end tens of thousands of lawsuits against Bayer, the German pharmaceutical and biotech giant, that claim the weedkiller Roundup caused non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Along with a favorable ruling from the U.S. Supreme Court this summer that barred Bayer from being sued in state courts for not putting a warning label on Roundup, the settlement is expected to largely end legal issues that have dogged Bayer for a decade.

“The Court’s final approval is a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation,” Bill Anderson, Bayer’s chief executive, said in a statement.

Bayer will pay the settlement into a fund over the next 21 years, and people making claims that Roundup caused their non-Hodgkin lymphoma will be eligible for payments of $10,000 to $165,000 depending upon the severity of their cancer, their ages, their occupations and other factors.

“Today’s final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice,” said Christopher Seeger, one of the lawyers for the plaintiffs.

Timothy Boyer, the Missouri circuit court judge overseeing the case, called the awards “fair and adequate” and said the settlement was “among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements.”

Bayer bought Monsanto, the St. Louis-based manufacturer of Roundup, in 2018 for $63 billion. Roundup is the most widely used herbicide in the world and is sprayed on hundreds of millions of acres of farmland annually that are planted with seeds genetically modified to tolerate Roundup.

But with that purchase, Bayer inherited a legal problem that eventually snowballed into around 170,000 lawsuits, with plaintiffs winning huge jury awards in courtrooms across the country.

Most of the cases focused on state failure-to-warn laws. Plaintiffs said Bayer should have put a warning label on Roundup saying it could cause cancer and that failing to do so violated laws in most states. Bayer argued that doing so would directly conflict with the label required by the federal Environmental Protection Agency, which regulates herbicides and had determined that Roundup was safe.

Eventually the Supreme Court agreed to hear the dispute. The Trump administration filed a brief supporting Bayer’s position, reversing the Biden administration’s position and infuriating activists from the Make America Healthy Against movement. The Supreme Court ruled 7 to 2 in Bayer’s favor.

Bayer and the plaintiffs preliminarily agreed to the settlement in February, before the Supreme Court heard the case. Lawyers for the plaintiffs said that a settlement was necessary because a Supreme Court ruling against them could leave their clients with nothing. For Bayer, a loss could have meant more suits and more expensive settlements. Mr. Anderson, the Bayer chief executive, said then that the settlement and a positive Supreme Court ruling would provide the “the tightest possible form of containment” to the lawsuits.

With Friday’s final approval of the settlement, Bayer will be able to put most Roundup lawsuits behind it, but the effort has been costly. The company has spent years litigating in courtrooms across the country and has settled tens of thousands of cases individually or in groups before this latest class action settlement.

Bayer previously said its litigation costs related to Roundup were at least $14 billion.

item.title: Why Nostalgia for Tamagotchis, the Needy Little Virtual Pets, Won’t Die
item.description:
Rachel Liew started collecting Tamagotchis in 2013, shortly after she graduated from college. Now 36, with a job in human resources, she owns more than 200 of the virtual pets.

“I love being able to be in a group of people who have the same interests as me,” said Liew, who lives in Singapore and considers herself part of the Tamagotchi’s global online fan community. “I can’t get that in real life.”

When Akihiro Yokoi had the idea for the toy in the mid-1990s, he didn’t know it would be a hit. Yokoi, who owned and operated the Japanese toy design studio Wiz Co., told The New York Times in 1997 that he had seen a commercial with a boy trying to take his pet turtle along on a trip. How nice it would be, Yokoi thought, if people had portable pets.

The pocket-size digital gadgets, which mimicked newborn baby chicks, required continuous care, feeding and attention and were among the first video games to be, initially, marketed primarily to girls. The Japanese edition of the Tamagotchi instruction manual was even made to resemble the health records mothers used to track their babies’ growth, Anne Allison wrote in “Millennial Monsters: Japanese Toys and the Global Imagination” (2006).

More than 100 million Tamagotchis have been sold since they first appeared in Japan in 1996 — more than 33 million of those in the United States, where they debuted a year later, the toy’s maker, Bandai Namco, said.

That number has continued to tick upward as the addictive egg-on-a-keychain has enjoyed a resurgence in popularity, particularly among millennial and Gen Z women. The TikTok creator Charli D’Amelio has been a global ambassador, and the KPop group BlackPink recently collaborated on a limited-edition version. (Around 40 percent of Tamagotchi owners are adults, according to a 2020 company survey.)

Julie Woodward, an organizer of the NYC Tamagotchi Club, said, “Something I hear quite often from people in New York City — who, like me, often live in very small apartments — is that they like nurturing virtual pets.” Woodward, 28, a content creator, added, “we get together and hang out and connect our devices.”

What is remarkable about the Tamagotchi is not only its cross-cultural appeal, but its longevity. While other virtual pets like Neopets and Webkinz have had comebacks, the Tamagotchi will not die. Last year its 38th model, the Tamagotchi Paradise, debuted, offering 51 characters across 12 species in nine languages and with Wi-Fi connectivity to friends’ devices and the online “Tamaverse.” (It still, though, requires two AAA batteries.)

Tamagotchis were available in dozens of North American countries by May 1997, as well as in Europe and parts of Asia. They proved so distracting that some schools banned them. Many mothers became de facto Tamagotchi moms, tasked with keeping their kids’ beloved pets alive while they were in class. (Tamagotchis die without proper care, but can be reset.)

The Tamagotchi would spend the next few years navigating the trend cycle and shifting consumer obsessions. By 1998, the virtual pets were already trying to fend off a fuzzy robot called the Furby — and sales were cooling from the staggering 70 million worldwide orders in 1997 alone.

But Bandai rolled out a new model, the Tamagotchi Connection, in 2004. It featured built-in infrared sensors that allowed owners to face off in mini-games, send messages, exchange gifts and even fall in love and get married.

“It’s driven by nostalgia, but when you add on today’s technology capabilities, I think they’ll actually end up being almost more fun today than they were 30 years ago,” said Peter Fader, a marketing professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, who focuses on consumer behavior.

Luke Williams, 40, a graphic designer for the National Health Service in Birmingham, England, appreciates the analog gameplay.

“It helps me stay grounded and focused, not distracted by notifications popping up on my screen all day,” he said.

In recent years, a passionate online fan community has sprung up around the toys. Content creators on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube review new models, showcase massive collections, and share video tutorials on painting, bedazzling and creating custom shells.

More than 60 in-person clubs have also formed, with chapters in Chile, Japan, Mexico, the Philippines, Singapore and the United States.

“It’s a fun way to connect with people all over the world,” said Twoey Gray, 31, the founder of the Toronto Tamagotchi Club, which has attracted as many as 100 people to its in-person meet-ups.

Bandai Namco plans to mark the toy’s anniversary in New York City with a Times Square takeover on Sunday. A free pop-up party with photo booths, product demonstrations and giveaways will be capped by a half-hour evening takeover of digital billboards across Times Square.

Woodward, the NYC Tamagotchi Club host, is planning to go.

“I’m excited to see everyone having a real-life encounter with Tamagotchi, all at once,” she said. “That’s going to be such a cool experience.”
