item.title: Inside the 350-Acre N.J. Campus Where Used Car Prices Are Set
item.description:
Car dealerships and Super Bowl ads are the most visible part of the auto industry. But arguably the real action is in places like this vast rectangular building near Trenton, N.J.

Hundreds of vehicles change hands on sale days at this auction center owned by Manheim, a division of Cox Automotive. It is among the largest of about 80 U.S. auction hubs Manheim operates.

The center has 17 lanes, each with its own entrance and exit. Manheim workers, many of them retirees earning a few extra bucks, drive vehicles slowly through garage-style doors, past auctioneers calling out prices from podiums, then out the other side. The din is overwhelming.

The site, in Bordentown, N.J., sells about 4,500 vehicles a week, part of a $730 billion market for used cars. Measured by the number of vehicles sold, the used car market is now more than double the size of the new car market. The vehicles might be trade-ins, coming off leases, older rental cars or repossessed from owners who fell behind on monthly loan payments.

Most Americans can’t afford new cars and have to buy used vehicles. In October, the average sale price for a new car was more than $51,000, according to Cox, a record. Automakers have discontinued many affordable models, like the Nissan Versa and the Ford Escape, because they were less profitable than big pickups and sport utility vehicles.

“You don’t see a lot of cars under $25,000,” said Lenny LaRocca, who leads the U.S. automotive industry practice at KPMG.

That has only made places like Manheim’s Bordentown hub more important. Auctions play a large role in setting prices for used cars, affecting the finances of millions of Americans.

Used car prices have been following the new car market higher. The average retail price of a three-year-old used car was $33,000 in October, up 2 percent from a year earlier. But there were big differences among categories.

Prices for electric vehicles and fuel-efficient compact cars rose more than 6 percent in October as buyers looked to save money on fuel. Prices for less efficient luxury cars, pickups and sport utility vehicles slipped, according to the Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index, a closely watched benchmark that is based on sales at Bordentown and other auction centers.

So far this year, wholesale prices for the least fuel-efficient cars have fallen 15 percent while prices for the most efficient vehicles have risen 10 percent. “Gas prices matter,” Jeremy Robb, chief economist at Cox Automotive, told several reporters during a tour of the center.

Sixteen of the 25 fastest-selling used cars are electric, according to separate data from iSeeCars, an online shopping site.

On a recent sunny day, car dealers, typically men dressed in jeans or sweatpants, roamed the auction lanes, stepping carefully to avoid the moving vehicles and indicating bids with a nod or a raised hand.

A blue Mercedes-Benz wagon with a badly dented right side went for $9,800. A 2023 Subaru Outback went for $14,800. A top-of-the-line BMW sport utility vehicle sold for almost $60,000.

“There she goes,” shouted an auctioneer, declaring the winning bid for the BMW by banging a length of rubber hose like a gavel. The vehicle disappeared through a door back into the sunlight.

Most of the bidding, about 70 percent, is done online. Before vehicles go on sale, they are driven through a brightly lit tunnel where 40 cameras capture detailed images that bidders can scrutinize. Manheim’s employees also inspect vehicles and flag problems.

“Unlike a new car, every used car is unique,” said Grace Huang, president of Cox Automotive’s Inventory Solutions group, who oversees the auction centers.

The New Jersey site has body and repair shops where vehicles can be spruced up. Manheim offers software to help sellers decide whether to make fixes or sell vehicles as they are.

Thousands of cars and trucks wait in parking lots that cover most of the 350-acre site. More than once, gangs of thieves have broken through the high fences, topped with barbed wire, and made off with valuable vehicles.

A growing percentage of cars at the lot were repossessed from owners who are struggling financially. Rising prices are forcing buyers to stretch their budgets, often to the breaking point. In October, 18 percent of car loans were subprime, meaning they were taken out by buyers with poor credit histories, according to Cox.

Signs point to a used car market that will continue to be lively. The average car on U.S. roads is 13 years old — older than they’ve ever been. Many people who have been putting off replacing their ride may not be able to wait much longer.

“Most vehicles are not made to last longer than 13 years,” Mr. Robb, the chief economist, said.

The used-car market is also becoming an important source of revenue for carmakers. They have discovered that they can make good money selling parts like floor mats or subscriptions to features like adaptive cruise control.

“A little known secret,” Mr. LaRocca of KPMG said, is that carmakers “actually make a lot of money in their aftermarket business.”

item.title: The Faces of the 2026 DealBook Summit
item.description:
Each year at the DealBook Summit, guests who speak on its main stage sit for portraits after their interviews with The New York Times columnist Andrew Ross Sorkin.

This year’s portraits, shown below, were made by the photographer Bryan Derballa.

Greg Brockman, a founder at OpenAI and its president, said at the summit,that artificial intelligence models “are now capable enough that we need to think about safety, security, alignment.” He spoke alongside Sam Altman, the co-founder and chief executive of OpenAI, pictured at top.

Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, said, “I see it as my duty to clarify, rectify and speak from my position and based on the experience that I’ve had.”

Satya Nadella, Microsoft’s chief executive, told Andrew that as artificial intelligence agents expose more vulnerabilities, digital infrastructure can have “essentially a nation-state-level persistent attacker going after you all the time, so that means we have a lot of fragility.”

Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York said: “I want the public sector to be so good that the people in this room, no matter how much money they may have in their pocket, will choose to use that public sector. And at its best, that’s what New York is.”

Adena Friedman, the chief executive of Nasdaq, said of A.I. giants, “These companies are remarkably consequential companies for the future of the economy, the future of society.”

“Mention markets are entertaining — that’s for sure,” said Vlad Tenev, the chief executive of Robinhood, whose company has banned such wagers. “But they’re also easy to manipulate.”

Palmer Luckey, the chief executive of Anduril, a defense technology company, said of war, “Life and death at scale is too morally fraught an area to not bring your absolute best tool to the table, even if it makes people feel icky.”

David Ellison, the chairman and chief executive of Skydance, said, “There are stories that impacted me dramatically when I was a kid, and to now be in a position to be able to be a part of telling those stories with the incredible filmmakers and showrunners that we get to work with is incredibly exciting.”

Hailey Bieber, the founder, chief creative officer and head of innovation of Rhode Skin, said: “I think social media really can be distorting. It can be distorting to the mind. It can be distorted, especially those filters that change your face — they make your lips bigger, your nose smaller. I do think that can definitely be harmful and misleading 100 percent, but it is, it’s part of the world we’re living in. It’s not going anywhere.”

“People have gravitated to that as an information source,” Polymarket’s chief executive Shayne Coplan said, referring to prediction markets. “And that’s the thing that I’m really excited about.”

item.title: My A.I. Hack Emergency Plan
item.description:
The warnings are coming thick and fast: Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, said that the Iranian government has its sights on U.S. energy, water and financial services systems.

Senior executives at A.I. companies say their tools could act on their own and wreak similar havoc — or human hackers could deploy A.I.

So imagine a nationwide power outage. Or consider a municipal water system that turns off or becomes unsafe. Maybe the internet stops working for a while, and a lot of important things that you are used to accessing on the fly — Waze for a teen driver to get home, Venmo to pay a caregiver — are suddenly unavailable.

There is no way to know the odds of any of this happening, but they are probably higher than they were a year ago. There is, as an Anthropic security executive put it recently, a “vulnerability tsunami” headed our way.

Some preparation seems prudent right about now.

Millions of people who are familiar with extreme weather already know the basic outlines of personal readiness. The rest of us probably don’t.

That included me and my underprepared family of four, in our midsize Brooklyn apartment building, until we made our own plans in recent weeks.

I am not a traditional “prepper,” and I didn’t exactly volunteer for this assignment. I’m a veteran personal finance columnist whose beat is beating the system. But editors know that when strange times necessitate resourcefulness — voting when you can’t get to the ballot box, chasing Covid vaccines when there’s a stampede for them, scoring scarce Bruce Springsteen tickets — I can help figure things out.

The federal government tells us all to be prepared to hunker down for three days as a general rule. It doesn’t take much more effort to be ready to fend for yourself for a week. And it stands to reason that if it has taken days to recover from weather-related blackouts or mistakes that result from minor telecommunications upgrades, it could take a week or more to solve problems that result from A.I.-enabled attacks.

So at least a week of readiness was my goal. Here’s what I planned and what I bought.

Also, rehearse. We intend to practice using everything we hadn’t owned before this month.

The people you love matter more than anything, so you’ll need a plan for where, how or if you’re going to meet up.

In the language of more traditional preppers, we hope to “bug in” and hunker down, not bug out and try to flee the city. A second home hours away with a month of firewood, a solar array and an ample natural spring is not our reality.

My wife also happens to be a colleague, so we’d make the seven-mile trek home together as efficiently as possible and collect our 11 year-old from school along the way.

Our other daughter is at college much of the year. If we’re unable to communicate, the plan is for her to stay in her apartment there, with friends, relying at first on whatever food the school could provide.

Although she’s within reasonable driving distance, she has no car, and the roads between here and there are already prone to gridlock. She would make her own call about whether to try to travel back to us after a few days, and only in a group for safety.

I’m also making her take the Rand McNally Road Atlas I got her for her 16th birthday back to school after Thanksgiving. Paper maps are scarce these days, but they shouldn’t be.

For at least the first few hours after a power outage, many stores would try to stay open temporarily. If electronic payments are impossible, having at least $500 in cash on hand in small bills would be useful. Build up to it over months if you need to, $20 bill by bill.

There may be outages that affect only the banking system and not the energy grid. If A.T.M.s or credit card terminals don’t work for a while — or your individual bank’s or region’s machinery is not functioning — you could need a fair bit of real money. Some Chase A.T.M.s were indeed not working when the bank had technical difficulties earlier this week.

The body needs more water, sooner, than it does food, so provisioning ought to start here in preparation for many types of outages. At the first sign of trouble, fill any bathtubs, sinks and containers.

A World Health Organization guide suggests a gallon of water per day, per person for consumption. Our plan: No bathing (though we usually have packages of baby wipes around), no cooking (unless we still have gas), no dishes, minimal flushing.

We chose to buy drinking water to have on hand just in case, which necessitates shelf Jenga and purges in our storage-constrained apartment.

If you rely on municipal water, you may want to purify it if you’re worried that it is unsafe. We’ve bought supplies for that, and my colleagues at Wirecutter offer advice on containers, water treatment and all manner of other emergency supplies.

Those of you with electricity-powered wells will need a backup plan for power or manual pumping.

A guide from W.H.O. and other agencies suggests 2,100 calories per person per day to meet basic survival needs. There are plenty of ways to achieve that for a week with a limited selection of nutrient-dense, shelf-stable food. We’ve got a supply of peanut butter, canned chicken, fruit purée packets, cooked chickpeas and ready-to-eat lentils — and a manual can opener.

You won’t be alone in those aisles of the store. This week, Costco’s chief financial officer told Bloomberg that the retailer has recorded higher sales of rice, water and generators in recent weeks.

If you have large solar panels on your house, power may not be a concern. Other homeowners install whole-house generators or have portable ones. None of that works for most apartment dwellers, including me.

The search for a power solution should begin with the problem, like whether an outage could disable medical equipment. Our family is lucky; we don’t need to keep life-sustaining gear running or take temperature-sensitive prescription drugs.

One concern for us is losing our electric heat. Portable power stations — which look like boomboxes or rolling suitcases, depending on their capacity — can help, though a space heater will drain them quickly. Portable solar panels can recharge the stations, but even in ideal weather with direct sunlight, the process is slow.

If it comes to it, our heating solution would be layers of clothing, clustering together and an electric blanket or two. We would draw electricity from a Jackery Explorer 300, a small power station we purchased that can also charge a phone or keep a fan or light running for a while. We added a small solar panel that is compatible with the Explorer that should allow us to at least partially recharge it.

Because we don’t plan to leave our home, we don’t have extra containers of gasoline. But I remember the lines after Hurricane Sandy, and we try to keep our car’s fuel tank full just in case.

Your own fuel needs could depend on how far you’d have to drive in a medical emergency if 911 and ambulances are not functioning well. If you regularly travel more than a few miles, consider what kind of supply kit should be in the car.

It’s hard to predict how quickly your fully charged mobile phone might cease to function as a communications device in the event of a widespread outage. The towers that carry signals have backup batteries, but they would not last long.

Staying online could keep you better informed than relying on a hand crank or solar-powered radio alone, though having one of those is a fine idea too.

In the early days of at-home internet service, I had two ways of accessing it given how frequently one or the other fritzed out. So I wondered whether Starlink might be a good backup for our household, which currently relies on two different companies for phone and Apple Watch connectivity plus Verizon for high-speed internet. Could Starlink help if some companies come under attack but others don’t?

Starlink’s website promises that you can set up a dish without a technician. I wanted to try, but my apartment’s layout would not allow the dish to connect with the company’s satellites. Its competitors’ websites offer larger dishes — too big to fit on my balcony.

If seven days minimum is the base line of good preparation, you’ll never want to have less than a week of any essential prescription medication on hand.

If your insurance company or pharmacy benefit manager makes this hard, talk to the person who prescribes your medicine and ask how best to stash away an emergency supply. Perhaps that person has some free samples.

The family checking account and our individual retirement accounts are at a large financial servicers provider. Our 401(k)s are at another.

In a prolonged attack, what proof will they have that we own what we own?

The company that holds our I.R.A.s pointed me to regulations that dictate its disaster planning. It must have records in a “write-only” format, so that no rogue robot could copy over the list of our holdings. There is redundancy to the records, and it must store backups separately.

The 401(k) company emailed me a statement. “We are closely tracking developments and risks associated with frontier A.I. We also use advanced A.I. tools to test and strengthen our own defenses and help us prepare for emerging threats. While the technology is evolving quickly, so are our defenses.”

Both companies post their business continuity plans publicly, and your brokerage firm is supposed to as well.

I also wondered about our life and home insurance provider. Would it be ready for losses on a large scale? It would not comment, and it would not tell me why.

I sometimes wonder what would happen if someone or something managed to knock Google Drive offline and keep it there. It doesn’t break often, so I’ve chosen not to worry. Still, this week I printed what I would most need and want.

For a more extensive guide to backing up your electronic life, see the article I wrote with colleagues last year when Elon Musk and his acolytes were probing federal databases, prompting fears they might break something important. Colleagues have also published extensive coverage this year on improving your password habits.

In reporting this story, many people surmised that after about a week of outages, order could break down. Good people would get desperate and start doing bad things. Would having a firearm be wise?

I haven’t taken up arms. Guns bring the risk of theft, accidents and self-harm in dark moments. Defending yourself requires training, practice, the courage to fire and a steady hand. I would be new at this. You may not be.

Even writing this down is psychologically corrosive. It’s also infuriating, given that the risks of rogue or hacked A.I. are human-made and the technology is making some of those humans fabulously wealthy.

So I’m choosing to tell myself the following things. I live in a building with kind neighbors in a community where people look out for one another. They too know that preparation is a form of community service. When things go sideways, you don’t want to be a burden. We saw this in the aftermath of Hurricane Sandy, and people remember.

As for those recent outages, a lot of them may have happened because I.T. heroes were frantically patching holes and erecting defenses to block bad actors and their A.I. weaponry. This is a positive sign — just as it is a foreboding one.

It has long been true here in my big city that big government, big finance, big power and big water are full of people whose primary job is to consider technical threats. They probe weaknesses proactively and alert one another to problems. They don’t want to fail, and they too do not wish to activate their personal emergency plans.

Also, some critical infrastructure managers are as fluent with A.I. tools as hackers are and can counterprogram against rogue bots. A.I. defense could fight A.I. offense to a worldwide draw, meaning nothing truly awful ever comes to pass.

And a reminder, though it seems a lifetime ago. Human beings brought another big, globe-straddling problem under control pretty recently. A Covid vaccine emerged in less than a year, for those who were willing to use it.

So you can either bet on the humans to outwit the robots within a week of a major incident or not. I’ve chosen my side — after stocking my shelves.

item.title: Anthropic’s Debut Shows the Disconnect Between Wall Street and Silicon Valley
item.description:
Anthropic on Thursday celebrated its first day of trading as stock prices surged and the company touched a valuation of $2 trillion. On Friday, its stock deflated, sinking 9 percent.

In the aftermath of its record-breaking initial public offering, Anthropic, which makes the Claude chatbot, has vacuumed up more than $120 billion in investor funds. It also consumed the good will of investors, many of whom were already becoming spooked at the artificial intelligence industry’s trillions of dollars of spending on data centers and other infrastructure to power the technology.

Following the huge investments in Anthropic, rival OpenAI and other A.I start-ups may face new hurdles going public, analysts and investors said. And even more established A.I. companies which need to raise debt or equity to pay for their expansion projects may encounter an uphill battle as the sector loses its glow.

That new hesitation was on full display this week, reflecting the widening disconnect between Silicon Valley optimism over A.I.’s potential and Wall Street’s growing doubts about whether the businesses are financially viable.

“The old-school way of looking at this is: This is the largest I.P.O. in history, late in the A.I. cycle. Psychologically, that could be a topping event,” said Michael O’Rourke, chief market strategist at JonesTrading, which brokers stock sales for hedge funds.

The market was shaken on Friday by some of those fears, ending the week with the worst stock slide in more than a year. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite fell 5.3 percent, wiping away the gains it had made this year. And the S&P 500 fell 3.7 percent, reaching correction territory, or a drop of 10 percent from its recent high.

Stocks of bellwether A.I. companies including Nvidia, CoreWeave and Advanced Micro Devices fell by double-digit percentages on Friday.

Contributing to the sell-off was last week’s resignation of Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, and worries about what that means for the chip maker’s important role financing other A.I. companies. Interest rates are also rising, making it more expensive for some companies to build data centers and buy chips. And Democrats swept into power during the midterm elections, many promising A.I. regulation.

Those developments put the enormous amount of money needed to finance the chips, data centers and electricity underpinning the technology at risk. Companies are planning to spend about $5 trillion between now and 2030 on the infrastructure, said Michael Arougheti, chief executive of Ares Management, a large investment manager, on an earnings call last month.

SpaceX, Meta and others tapped the markets last month for tens of billions of dollars to fuel their A.I. spending. Executives at most tech giants have told investors they are increasing their spending on the technology each quarter. And Anthropic’s initial public offering piled on top, causing fatigue, analysts and investors said.

Many concerns about A.I. spending are easily dismissed in Silicon Valley, which, by nature, lives in a different world. Venture capitalists this year have minted nearly 200 new unicorns, or start-ups worth more than $1 billion, more than in any other year since the private market frenzy in 2021, according to PitchBook, which tracks start-ups.

But a market for the kinds of initial public offerings or mergers to justify the velocity of investments hasn't yet emerged.

Even in Anthropic’s case, the company allowed early employees to sell more than $25 billion of combined stock at the start of trading, an unusually large sum that some investors and analysts viewed as aggressive. Companies and their investment bankers usually limit employees and other shareholders from selling their stock for weeks or months after I.P.O.s to help stabilize the price.

Many hedge fund managers failed to get stock in Anthropic’s offering at the initial price of $83 per share, said Raphaëlle D’Ornano, an A.I. industry analyst who also invests in public stocks. The hedge funds instead paid a significantly higher price for shares when trading opened on Thursday at $111.50.

Those hedge funds would have lost money as the stock quickly sank, closing at $88.91 on Friday. At the same time, funds have been trying to limit how much stock they own in A.I. companies overall, she added.

Friday “was pure panic,” Ms. D’Ornano said.

Wall Street and Silicon Valley largely agree that A.I. tools are certain to upend how people work, use the internet, and maybe even make discoveries in medicine. But no one is confident on how quickly the technology will produce those benefits.

And as the tech companies invest heavily, it isn’t clear how many will bring in enough revenue to become profitable. Anthropic’s rapid revenue growth has depended on businesses that use Claude for automating software engineering work, and the company will need to broaden that customer base in the coming years, analysts said.

OpenAI, which has filed for an initial public offering expected as soon as next year, is hoping for a similar shift into a broader customer base. The company also wants to get more free users of its popular chatbot, ChatGPT, to start paying.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Those business realities have led to some criticism from Wall Street fund managers, who feel that many in Silicon Valley are overly optimistic about potential returns. For example, Dylan Patel, a closely followed A.I. industry analyst, has predicted unrelenting growth, saying Anthropic and OpenAI would together surpass a half-trillion dollars in revenue by the end of next year, despite shaky markets.

As Mr. Patel walked onstage at a private San Francisco conference for venture capitalists and start-up founders this month to an upbeat electronic song, “Levels” by Avicii, tech stocks were tanking. “Do you have more depressing music, given what’s going on in the market?” he joked.

Mr. Patel, who runs the San Francisco-based market research company SemiAnalysis, said at the conference that investors’ skepticism about the continued pace of revenue growth at OpenAI and Anthropic was one big reason for market turmoil. He predicted those companies would generate more revenue from new business lines, like offering cybersecurity tools and designing chips.

“I myself am a little cuckoo, and I think they actually will hit this, just to be clear,” he said. “But I think many people are a bit skeptical.”

Some A.I. start-up executives said they have noticed a pullback from investors as they consider jumping into their next rounds of funding. Those company leaders are starting to openly acknowledge one awkward reality of the A.I. boom: The technology’s growth has been largely powered by a relatively small number of voracious business customers and consumers who pay for it.

“Eighty percent of the revenue is probably coming from 20 percent of the users. It might even be 90 percent,” said Aravind Srinivas, the chief executive of the Nvidia-backed A.I. start-up Perplexity, at a conference last week hosted by the tech publication, Newcomer.

(The Times has sued Perplexity, accusing it of copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The company has denied the claims.)

Even as Silicon Valley venture capitalists watched Anthropic’s rocky entry into the public markets, they remained upbeat about the future.

Hemant Taneja, the chief executive of tech investment firm General Catalyst, said he felt relief that Anthropic’s stock price held above the offering price amid “turbulent” markets. Anthropic, he added, was not a one-off example of a venture-funded company that would capitalize on A.I. advances.

“I’m walking away saying: Who’s the next set of founders with the same opportunity?” he said.
